options: Yes, std::random
No — the rand crate is the ecosystem standard
Yes, but only for integers, not floats
Only on the nightly compiler
quiz.explain: Generating good randomness is its own algorithmic problem, so it lives in the rand crate rather than std.

quiz.q: Why does calling `.choose()` on a slice fail with 'no method named `choose` found' if you've only written `use rand::Rng;`?
options: choose() doesn't exist anywhere in the rand crate
.choose() lives on the rand::seq::SliceRandom trait, which must be imported separately
You must call rand::rng() before importing anything
Slices in Rust can never be randomized
quiz.explain: Rng and SliceRandom are two different traits for two different jobs — generating numbers vs. doing something random with a collection.

quiz.q: Why would you use `StdRng::seed_from_u64(42)` instead of `rand::rng()`?
options: It's faster to generate numbers with
It's the only RNG type that supports random_range
It produces the exact same sequence every run — useful for tests and simulations
It's required before you can call .shuffle()
quiz.explain: A seeded RNG is fully reproducible, which is exactly what you want when a test or simulation needs to be deterministic.

quiz.q: Which trait must be in scope to call `.shuffle()` on a `Vec`?
options: rand::Rng
rand::seq::SliceRandom
std::cmp::Ord
serde::Serialize
quiz.explain: shuffle() and choose() both live on SliceRandom, a trait separate from Rng.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you assume the default `rand::rng()` is safe for generating security tokens?
options: It's too slow for that kind of use case
Its default algorithm is built for speed and statistical quality, not guaranteed unpredictability against an attacker
It can only generate numbers between 0 and 100
rand doesn't support any security-related use case, period
quiz.explain: Statistical randomness and cryptographic unpredictability are different properties — check rand's docs before using it for tokens or secrets.

quiz.q: What risk does a test built directly on `rand::rng()` (the default thread RNG) carry?
options: It will fail to compile inside a #[test] function
Flaky results, since different runs can draw different random values
It always runs noticeably slower than other tests
It can never be used alongside assert! macros
quiz.explain: The default RNG is intentionally unpredictable — great for real use, bad for a test that needs to behave the same way every run.

flashcards.front: Does std have a random number generator?
flashcards.back: No — the rand crate is the ecosystem standard.

flashcards.front: How do you get a random number from 1 to 6, inclusive?
flashcards.back: rng.random_range(1..=6) — the ..= makes the range inclusive so 6 is actually reachable.

flashcards.front: What trait do .choose() and .shuffle() require in scope?
flashcards.back: rand::seq::SliceRandom — without importing it, those methods don't exist on a slice.

flashcards.front: What does slice.choose(&mut rng) return, and why?
flashcards.back: Option<&T> — None when the slice is empty, since there's nothing to pick.

flashcards.front: How do you get a reproducible sequence of 'random' numbers?
flashcards.back: Seed a specific generator, e.g. StdRng::seed_from_u64(42), instead of using the default rand::rng().

flashcards.front: Is the default rand::rng() safe for generating security tokens?
flashcards.back: Not guaranteed — check rand's docs for a CSPRNG before using randomness for tokens, session ids, or secrets.

flashcards.front: Why seed an RNG inside a test?
flashcards.back: So the test's random input is identical every run, avoiding flakiness from whatever values the default RNG happened to draw.
